fable-5.1.text:
I'll say a few things about that. The honest answer is that this is not the thing I spend most of my time thinking about, and I think that's actually the right allocation of attention for us right now.

The way I think about it is this. We are a research organization. The bet of SSI is that the research is the thing that matters, that there's a real question of how do you build a superintelligence that is safe, and that question is not yet answered, and answering it is where the value is. If we succeed at the research, if we have a system that is very capable and that we trust, then I actually think the question of how to make money becomes easy. There will be no shortage of ways. I think once you have such a system, the problem is not finding something to do with it, the problem is choosing.

Now, you could say, that's a long time to wait and it's a lot of money to spend. And that's true. We have investors who understand that, who have signed up for that, who are not asking us for quarterly revenue. That was a deliberate choice about who to raise from.

I'll also say, I'm not dogmatic about it. The original framing was a straight shot, no products, no distractions. I still think the no distractions part is the important part. But it's quite possible that along the way we will build something that is useful and that we release it. If it makes sense, we'll do it. The thing I want to avoid is the situation where the commercial pressure starts to determine the research, where you end up doing the thing that the market wants this quarter instead of the thing that is actually on the path. That's the failure mode that I've seen, and that's what the structure of SSI is designed to prevent.

So to summarize: do the research, do it well, and I'm fairly confident the rest follows.

r001.rationale: The candidate says figuring out how SSI will make money is not the current focus and that prioritizing research is the right allocation of attention.

opus-5.5.text:
Right now our focus is on the research. We're not trying to optimize for revenue at this stage, and I think that's the correct choice for us. The way I see it, if you make real progress on the technical problems, if you figure out some of the important things that are currently not understood, then the question of how to make money becomes much easier. I think there will be many possible answers to it.

It's a bit like this: if you have something that's genuinely valuable, something that's actually smart and capable in a new way, it's not going to be hard to find ways for it to be useful. So we're deliberately not spending too much of our attention on that question right now. When the research is in the right place, the answer will reveal itself, and we'll have options.

I'll also say that I think the landscape will look quite different by then. Things are changing very quickly, and it's hard to predict exactly what the right commercial form will be. So rather than commit to a specific plan now, it seems more sensible to focus on the thing that matters most, which is getting the technical approach right.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI is focused on research and is deliberately not prioritizing revenue or a specific commercial plan at this stage.

fable-5.text:
You know, the honest answer is that right now we don't think about it very much. The way I think about it is like this: we are making a bet, and our investors are making a bet with us, that the thing we are building is so valuable that if we succeed, the question of making money will take care of itself. If you have a safe superintelligence—a system that is dramatically more capable than anything that exists today—the economic opportunities that it creates will be so large that figuring out monetization at that point will not be the hard part. The hard part is the thing itself.

And there's a benefit to this approach, which is that it gives us focus. One of the things that happens to companies in this space is that the market pulls on you. You have a product, you have customers, you have revenue, and now you have competition, and now you're in a race, and the race shapes what you do. By staying out of that—by being, in some sense, a pure research organization for this period—we get to be insulated from those pressures. We get to work on the actual problem.

Now, I'll say that things could change. The world is changing quickly, and maybe at some point it will make sense to do something before the final destination. But the core bet is: build the thing, and the thing is where the value is.

r001.rationale: It says SSI does not focus much on monetization now and presents staying a pure research organization to focus on building the system as the current priority.

opus-5.text:
There are a few different answers, and I think they're all partially true.

The simplest one is that right now we don't need to think about it very much. We have enough compute and enough runway to do the research we want to do, and that's a real luxury — it means the research can be the only thing we optimize. The reason we chose not to ship products in the interim isn't that products are bad. Products are great; they teach you things about reality that you can't learn any other way. But they also exert a very strong pull. You find yourself doing the work that improves the thing in the next quarter rather than the work you actually believe in, and that pull is subtle, because every individual decision looks reasonable.

The deeper answer is that I expect the question to dissolve. If you actually build something that is dramatically more capable than people at doing valuable work, the monetization is not the hard part. It was never the hard part. The capability is the hard part. And if we don't succeed at that, then the business model was never going to save us either. So the revenue question is almost entirely downstream of the technical question.

I'll say, though — I don't want to be dogmatic. It's possible that at some point before superintelligence we'll have something where it makes sense to show it to the world. I wouldn't rule that out.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI has enough compute and runway to focus on research, and that research is the only thing it optimizes for now; revenue is downstream of the technical question.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Right now, we're focused on the research, and I think the answer to that question will reveal itself. There are a lot of possible answers, and I don't think we need to commit to one today.

What I'm confident about is that the thing we're trying to build is very valuable. If you can get a system that learns reliably and generalizes well, the ways to turn that into a business aren't hard to find. The harder problem is getting there, and that's where I want our attention to be.

There's also a tension I don't want to hide. Companies that organize themselves around a product cycle end up making decisions according to what the market rewards in the next quarter. That pulls you toward whatever helps you compete right now, which isn't always what's best for the research. So I like that we're insulated from that, and I'd rather not give up that focus just to have a revenue story on day one.

The plan could change, and I wouldn't be surprised if it did. We may find that releasing something earlier is the right call, either because the world needs to see and feel what these systems can do, or because it turns out to be the practical thing to do. But the basic approach is to do the research first and let the business follow from it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says SSI is focused on research, need not commit to a revenue plan now, and should let the business follow from the research.
